terminal_record.title: Evercore to buy American Media; David Pecker named chairman and CEO
terminal_record.description_short: Evercore was buying American Media, publisher of the National Enquirer and Star; David Pecker was hired to lead the parent company.
terminal_record.description_medium: An Associated Press report carried by The Washington Post said Evercore Partners was buying American Media, publisher of the National Enquirer and Star, in a $300 million deal that also assumed debt. The Los Angeles Times reported that David Pecker, then chief executive of Hachette Filipacchi Magazines, was hired as American Media’s chairman and chief executive. The sources describe an Evercore-led acquisition and Pecker’s appointment; they do not establish a Trump-related purpose.
terminal_record.description_long: On February 17, 1999, The Washington Post published an Associated Press report saying Evercore Partners was buying American Media Inc., the publisher of the National Enquirer and Star. The report described a $300 million purchase and said Evercore would assume $470 million in debt. A Los Angeles Times report the same day said David Pecker, then head of Hachette Filipacchi Magazines, had been hired as American Media’s chairman and chief executive. The reports describe Evercore as the buyer of the parent publisher; Pecker was appointed to lead the company rather than shown as the individual buyer of the Enquirer. These reports correct the central ownership description. They do not establish that the paper was Mafia-owned, explain its earlier financing, or show a Trump-related purpose or connection in 1999. This card is limited to the corporate transaction and Pecker’s appointment as a contextual record. Any later political relationship involving Pecker requires its own evidence and should not be implied as the motive for this acquisition.

terminal_record.description_long: The supplied entry alleges that the Trump administration ended CDC grants and programs related to abortion research, contraception, and reproductive health in February 2025. It claims that programs for contraception counseling, teen pregnancy prevention, and maternal-health research lost funding, and that researchers had awards canceled mid-study. The same account predicts disproportionate effects on low-income and rural patients and reports advocates’ concern about unintended pregnancies; these are supplied claims, not documented outcomes in this draft. The available TAGGS excerpt shows one CDC award with a later 2025 termination date, involving birth defects and pregnant and postpartum health. It does not identify a February-wide action or show that all grants in these areas ended. The supplied information therefore does not establish the date, recipients, program scope, or effects of the alleged cancellation. No claim is made here that the listed programs were all terminated.
